details:
The web application uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. When the player opens the game, all data from it gets saved temporarily, and gets deleted when the session is closed or refreshed. This makes the game easy to launch and play again, without needing any manual intervention. Upon launch, the player chooses whether they want to launch a Lunar mission or a Martian mission. The game will inform them of the status each infrastructure station is in, and they have to assign crew members to each station in order to keep them operational and make them produce results efficiently. Each station comes at an operational cost considering power, water or human resources. Players need to understand how to divide resources in order to keep the outpost operational and at least one astronaut alive. 

The main benefit our game has is that it is very simple and easy to use, in compatibility with our target audience being children aged 7 - 12 years old. That is because clear instructions are provided in every part of the game, in order for the player to always be informed about what they are supposed to do in the current state they are in and it is also very easily replayable, by just refreshing the page of the game. It is also attractive, as it is filled with graphics and icons, the main of which is the virtual simulator at the top of the page that visualizes every change made by the player. Moreover, it is completely free and no sign up is required, as the project is open source and hosted on GitHub Pages and can be found from anywhere with no constraints. Furthermore, it is based on the real world application of a mission to the Moon or Mars, while at the same time it helps players understand the opportunity cost of their choices.

As a team, the impact we intend for our game to have is for players to be more familiar with the circumstances of a mission to the Moon or Mars and to understand that every choice and change comes with an opportunity cost. Organization and efficiency are keywords for a mission like this to succeed. Players are prompted to think strategically, think ahead and make decisions that could lead the mission for the better or for the worse. It is up to them to decide what is the best choice based on the current circumstances, in order to keep as many crew members alive until sol 30 as possible. 

The web application is coded in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used the Visual Studio Code IDE to run, test and debug the code, using the suitable extensions for HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We then combined the separate files to have the final result, which is our current web game. We tested the project on Mozilla Firefox for Linux and Android, as well as Google Chrome for MacOS. We are positive that it is functional for Safari and any other Firefox-based or Chromium-based web browser. The project is hosted on GitHub Pages and the code is open source and can be found here. Lastly, we used Claude to help us identify and fix some bugs that came around during the production of the visual simulator, which was one of the most challenging parts of the game’s creation.

Our project combines an educational and fun game with real world data in order to give players a better understanding on how a Lunar or Martian outpost will function. The idea is that players get to make decisions regarding a Lunar or Martian outpost that will ultimately decide whether the mission will be a success or a total failure. As mentioned above, every decision comes with an opportunity cost. We believe that turning all this into a fun and educational game will be easier for our target audience to learn about such missions, the risks and ultimately that decisions matter, whether they are for the best or for the worst. Everything that changes how the outpost functions is displayed at the top graphic, which is made simply so that even players who don't quite understand the numbers will know if the outpost is operational, or if there is an ongoing weather event etc.

Last but not least, there were many factors considered by our team during the creation of the game. Specifically, we considered the time constraints and to address the challenge, we created a well organized and time - specific plan to make sure we do not fall behind on any aspect of the project. Also, we are not trying to hide that we also did consider our limited knowledge, due to which we faced some challenges during production. Nevertheless, we faced those challenges by considering resources provided by NASA online. Most importantly, we did consider our target audience, which is children aged from 7 to 12 years old, in order for the game to be easily playable by kids of that age. For that reason we made sure to include visual graphics, vibrant colors and easy and clear instructions for every part of the game. This way, the gaming experience becomes fun and enjoyable!
